TITLE: Growing season carbon dioxide and methane exchange at a restored peatland on the Western Boreal Plain
SPECIES: T1=Sphagnum fuscum (Sphagnum moss); T2=Eriophorum vaginatum (E. vaginatum); T3=Polytrichum strictum (P. strictum); T4=Sphagnum angustifolium (S. angustifolium); T5=Carex aquatilis; T6=Carex canescens; T7=Ledum groenlandicum; T8=Oxycoccus microcarpus; T9=Picea mariana; T10=Pohlia nutans; T11=Rubus chamaemorus; T12=Salix pedicellaris; T13=Smilacina trifolia; T14=Sphagnum magellanicum
CONTEXT: The goal of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of restoration techniques based on [ref] as applied on a cutover peat bog in northern Alberta. Based on previous research on restored peatlands in Québec we hypothesized that: (1) restoration would decrease the CO2 source from peat fields and possibly result in a CO2 sink, (2) restoration would increase CH4 efflux and (3) water table and plant cover would be significant controls on rates of GHG exchange. Measurements were made across the ~ 10 ha restored section and compared to measurements at a neighboring unrestored section. The study site is situated in the Boreal Plains ecozone (Ecological Stratification Working Group, 1996). The restored site is owned and operated by Sun Gro Horticulture and had been previously drained by a series of ditches around the site and crossing it longitudinally along its major axis. This area was previously under active vacuum-extraction and was restored by the site operator in 2008 according to the North American Peatland Restoration Guide by [ref]. Briefly, restoration involved filling ditches on the restored area, spreading diaspores from a neighboring ombrotrophic bog in a ratio of 1:10 (1 ha of collected material over 10 ha of restored area), covering material with straw mulch, adding phosphate rock fertilizer ( 150 kg ha-1), and blocking perimeter ditches. Twelve sample plots were established systematically on the restored site (R) in approximately four rows (A–D) of three collars with each row spaced ~100 m apart along a main transect west to east along the site's major axis on the south side of the field (Fig. 1). The first row was ~\!100 m due east of the site access road. At the unrestored site only ER was determined as no vegetation was present.
TEXT:
[1] (abs) Boreal peatlands represent globally important long term sinks of carbon; however, horticultural peat extraction disrupts this carbon sink function, converting these ecosystems to large sources of greenhouse gases.
[2] (abs) Peatland restoration mitigates these emissions but to date no measurement of greenhouse gas exchange has been conducted on restored peatlands in western Canada, a region where continental climate could impact restoration success.
[3] (abs) We measured CO2 and CH4 fluxes during the growing season in a restored, cutover peatland in northern Alberta (Boreal Plain Ecozone) and compared these to fluxes measured on a neighboring unrestored area.
[4] (abs) Restoration resulted in a shiftin mean growing season fluxes from 378 g CO2 C and −0.2 g CH4 C at the unrestored site to −30 g CO2 C and 3.7 g CH4 C at the restored site, where positive values indicate flux of carbon from the peatland to the atmosphere.
[5] (abs) Carbon dioxide exchange was correlated to vascular vegetation cover that varied depending on local water table position.
[6] (abs) Water table was also related to CH4 flux, with higher emissions from wet sites.
[7] (abs) Restoration activities should avoid creating very dry microsites where greenhouse gas emissions will remain high, while very wet sites may accumulate carbon as CO2 but will likely create areas of high CH4 flux.

[10] (res) At both sites water table position was highest in July 2011, gradually declined into September 2011, remained low in spring 2012, but recovered slightly by July 2012.
[11] (res) At all plots the frost table was within the upper 25 cm during May 2012 measurements.
[12] (res) While the restored site soil thawed by late June 2012, the frost table remained within the upper 70 cm at the unrestored site into the July sampling date in 2012.
[13] (res) Restored plots had plant cover between 35 and 160%, most of which consist of spontaneously regenerated species.
[14] (res) Common species observed on the restored site included Carex aquatilis, Carex canescens, Eriophorum vaginatum, Salix pedicellaris, Polytrichum strictum and Pohlia nutans.

[32] (res) Ecosystem respiration was also significantly different between sites (df=2, F=5.56, p=0.02) with wet restored plots being significantly higher than unrestored plots.
[33] (res) Dry restored plots were not statistically significantly different from either wet restored or unrestored plots.
[34] (res) Combining all sites and using mean growing season values of $CO_2$ exchange and water table position, $GEP{max}$ and $NEE{max}$ were both significantly related to water table (linear regression, p < 0.05).

[36] (res) Although not significantly related to water table position alone, inclusion of this parameter with $GEP{max}$ in multiple regression explained an additional 11% of the variation in ER between sample plots (linear regression, $R^2(adj) = 0.78$, p < 0.001).
[37] (res) The correlation between ER and $GEP{max}$ was further supported by a significant linear regression between ER and vascular plant cover (Fig. 4, $R^2(adj) = 0.28$, p = 0.024).
[38] (res) Vascular plant cover was also a significant predictor of $log(GEP{max})$ (Fig. 4, linear regression, $R^2(adj) = 0.49$, p = 0.007).

[44] (res) Wet restored plots had significantly higher CH4 flux than dry restored plots (Mann–Whitney, p = 0.006).

[45] (res) Mean seasonal CH4 flux varied with water table with log (total season CH4 flux + 1) increasing as mean season water table position became shallower (Fig. 5; $R^2$ (adj)=0.25, p=0.057).

[47] (dis) Ongoing research on greenhouse gas exchange following peatland rewetting and restoration suggests that these activities greatly reduce carbon and greenhouse gas losses to the atmosphere and may return peatlands to carbon sinks over time.
[48] (dis) On the other hand, rewetting and colonization by aerenchymatous species (e.g. Carex spp, Eriophorum spp) can lead to large increases in CH4 flux.
[49] (dis) The present study supports these trends with restoration resulting in a shift in mean growing season net CO2 and CH4 fluxes from 378 g CO2—C and -0.2 g CH4—C at the unrestored site to -30 g CO2—C and 3.7 g CH4—C at the restored site.

(2013) report annual NEE and $CH_4$ fluxes of -14 to -588 g $CO_2$ —C m-2 and 5-12 g $CH_4$ —C m-2 for vegetated microsites and $37-82 \text{ g CO}2 \text{ m}^{-2}$ and $0.1 \text{ g CH}4$ –C m-2 for bare peat areas on a rewetted cutover peatland in Ireland restored 7-10 yr prior to the study.
[52] (dis) Growing season NEE in a cutover peatland in Finland 1-3 yr following rewetting was 44 to $-65 \,\mathrm{g}\,\mathrm{CO}2$ –C m-2.
[53] (dis) As with the present study, Tuittila et al. (1999) also reported a link between vascular plant cover and wetness resulting in increased CO2 sequestration in wetter zones.
[54] (dis) Methane efflux during the growing season from the same study site was $0.4-1.0 \,\mathrm{g\,CH_4-C\,m^{-2}}$ in the third year following rewetting.
[55] (dis) Samaritani et al. (2011) report growing season NEE for 29, 42 and 51 yr old regenerating plots on a cutover bog in the Swiss Jura mountains of 40, –222 and –209 g CO2−C m-2, respectively.
[56] (dis) In Canada, Waddington et al. (2010) report development of a growing season CO2 sink of $-20\,\mathrm{g}\,\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$ in the third year post-restoration for a restored cutover bog in Quebec, while CH4 emissions in the same year were $3.1 \,\mathrm{g\,CH_4-C\,m^{-2}}$.
[57] (dis) These values are similar to those reported in the present study suggesting that the continental climate does not greatly impact the effect of restoration on CO2 and CH4 fluxes, at least in the short term.
[58] (dis) Based on measurements at the same Quebec site 10 yr after restoration, Strack and Zuback (2013) determined that the site was annually a source of $102 \text{ g CO}2$ –C m-2 and $0.8 \text{ g CH}4$ –C m-2, likely due to the dry conditions during the study period.
[59] (dis) This illustrates the sensitivity of greenhouse gas flux estimates to the weather during the study period (e.g. Roulet et al., 2007; Urbanová et al., 2013) indicating the importance of long-term studies to determine robust estimates of peatland carbon balance.

[65] (dis) This probably occurred due to the peat chemistry on the site that has pH in surface water and shallow subsurface water of 6.71 and 5.39.
[66] (dis) This pH is higher than would be found in ombrotrophic conditions (bog pH 3.9-4.0, Vitt et al., 1995) and may indicate more minerotrophic or fen-like conditions on site.
[67] (dis) This often occurs for cutover peatlands if a large portion of the Sphagnum peat layer is removed resulting in extraction down to former fen peat.
[68] (dis) Vegetation surveys on abandoned cutover fens indicate that these sites are more likely to spontaneously re-vegetate than cutover bogs, particularly when drainage is blocked.
[69] (dis) Thus, when planning peatland restoration it is important for managers to measure chemistry of the residual peat and choose an appropriate donor site to increase the likelihood of propagule survival, and reduce cost and effort on sites where application of donor material may not be required.
[70] (dis) Despite the fact that most plants on the restored site likely did not result from the donor material, cover of both mosses and vascular plants was similar to that reported for other peatland restoration projects in Canada.
[71] (dis) For example, Graf et al. (2012) report mean total moss cover for nine restored peatlands near Rivière-du-Loup, Québec, Canada at $\sim$ 20% and total vegetation cover for the same sites at just over 30% 3 yr post-restoration.
[72] (dis) The presence of many wetland species not characteristic of bogs following restoration has also be reported in previous studies.

TEXT:
[73] (dis) Although spontaneous revegetation can occur following peatland extraction, moss cover often remains low.
[74] (dis) Mosses are important components of many undisturbed peatlands, make a major contribution to peat accumulation, and Sphagnum has been called a keynote genus for peatland restoration.
[75] (dis) Because of the very different porosity and water retention of near surface Sphagnum moss, newly formed Sphagnum moss carpets on restored cutover peatlands and the residual cutover peat, establishment of a thick new Sphagnum moss layer appears critical to return hydrologic function to restored sites.
[76] (dis) However, it remains unclear how important this near-surface moss layer is for fen hydrology.
[77] (dis) On the other hand, the present study highlights the importance of vascular plants, particularly graminoid cover in this case, for carbon sequestration.
[78] (dis) This has been reported elsewhere, with E. vaginatum often playing an important role in initial high rates of CO2 uptake following restoration.
[79] (dis) Yli-Petäys et al. (2007) even suggest that reduced rates of CO2 uptake several decades following restoration are partially linked to reduction in vascular plant cover.
[80] (dis) Thus, while a return to long-term ecohydrological function of restored peatlands, particularly bogs, likely requires successful moss establishment, vascular plants clearly play an important role in post-restoration carbon sequestration.
[81] (dis) On the other hand, vascular plant litter is generally more easily decomposed compared to moss litter and bogs have been reported to accumulate peat at greater rates than fens.
[82] (dis) However, Bauer et al. (2003) actually report greater rates of peat accumulation for rich fen areas compared to Sphagnum dominated areas in a peatland complex of the Western Boreal Plain.
[83] (dis) While these differences were likely hydrologically driven as Sphagnum dominated areas tend to have deeper water tables than rich fens in this region, results do indicate that fen-type vegetation can result in relatively rapid accumulation of peat with large herbaceous contribution.
[84] (dis) Evaluating the importance of mosses for long term rates of peat accumulation will require both year round monitoring of carbon fluxes and monitoring of restored sites for longer periods post-restoration.
[85] (dis) Graminoid cover accounted for a large proportion of total plant cover and was correlated to water table position, and this was likely an important driver for the relationship between water table and CO2 exchange.
[86] (dis) However, Chimner and Cooper (2003) report water table control on graminoid net primary productivity in a mountain fen suggesting that shallow water table is also likely to result in higher GEP once plants are established.
[87] (dis) Water table also largely controls CH4 flux (this study, Couwenberg and Fritz, 2012) and thus, while wet restored sites were larger seasonal sinks for CO2, they were also much larger sources of CH4.
[88] (dis) As peatland restoration may be implemented with a goal to reduce GHG emissions from disturbed sites, it is important to consider the impact of management decisions on resulting greenhouse gas budgets.While on average restoration reduced GWP from CO2 and CH4 at both dry and wet restored plots, both very dry and very wet plots remained GHG sources due to continued high emissions of CO2 (dry sites) or high CH4 efflux (wet sites).
[89] (dis) Total GHG balance in a peatland will also depend on fluxes of nitrous oxide (N2O), which was not measured in this study.
